sections.passage: A conversation between a tourist and a travel agent at a tourism office. The tourist, Mrs. Chen, is visiting from Taiwan and wants to book a multi-day tour of the Scottish Highlands. The travel agent, Andrew, welcomes her and asks about her preferences and schedule. Mrs. Chen explains that she has five days available, from Monday the 15th to Friday the 19th of June, and she is particularly interested in scenic landscapes, historic castles, and traditional Scottish culture. Andrew recommends the Highland Explorer Tour, which is their most popular five-day itinerary. He explains that the tour departs daily from Edinburgh at 8 AM in a comfortable coach with a maximum of twenty passengers, ensuring a more personal experience. The tour includes visits to several iconic locations. On day one, the group travels to Stirling Castle and then through the Trossachs National Park, stopping at Loch Lomond for a photo opportunity. The overnight stay is at a three-star hotel in Fort William. Day two includes a visit to the Glenfinnan Viaduct, famous for its appearance in the Harry Potter films, followed by a trip to the Isle of Skye. The group stays overnight in Portree, the main town on the island. Day three is spent exploring the Isle of Skye, including the Old Man of Storr rock formation and the Fairy Pools, a series of crystal-clear rock pools at the foot of the Black Cuillin mountains. Day four involves travelling through the dramatic landscape of Glencoe, stopping at a traditional whisky distillery for a tasting session, before returning to Fort William. The final day includes a visit to the medieval town of Dunkeld and the Hermitage forest walk before returning to Edinburgh by 6 PM. Mrs. Chen asks about the cost. Andrew tells her that the standard package costs 695 pounds per person, which includes all accommodation, breakfast each morning, two evening meals, all transportation in the coach, and the services of an English-speaking guide. For an additional 85 pounds, she can upgrade to a single room supplement, as the standard price is based on twin-sharing accommodation. Mrs. Chen also asks about optional activities. Andrew mentions that on the Isle of Skye, there is an optional boat trip to see sea eagles and seals for 35 pounds, and on day four, there is an optional guided hike in Glencoe for 20 pounds. Mrs. Chen says she would like to book the tour with the single room supplement and both optional activities. Andrew calculates the total cost and confirms it comes to 835 pounds. He asks for a 20 percent deposit of 167 pounds to secure the booking, with the balance due two weeks before departure. Mrs. Chen pays by credit card and receives her booking confirmation by email.

sections.passage: A talk by the curator of a museum introducing a new exhibition on ancient Egyptian civilisation. Good morning, everyone. My name is Dr. Catherine Brooks, and I am the senior curator of the Ancient World Gallery here at the National Museum. I am thrilled to welcome you to the preview of our new exhibition, Treasures of the Nile: 3,000 Years of Egyptian Civilisation, which opens to the public this Saturday. This exhibition has been three years in the making and represents the largest collection of Egyptian artefacts ever displayed in this country. The exhibition is organised chronologically across eight galleries and features over 400 objects, many of which have never been displayed outside of Egypt before. We are particularly grateful to the Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities for their generous loan of these extraordinary pieces. Gallery One, titled Dawn of the Pharaohs, covers the Predynastic and Early Dynastic periods from approximately 5000 to 2700 BC. Here you will see some of the earliest examples of Egyptian art and craftsmanship, including beautifully carved stone vessels, ivory combs, and a remarkable ceremonial palette depicting the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Galleries Two through Four trace the development of Egyptian civilisation through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. Highlights include a gilded funerary mask from the Eighteenth Dynasty, approximately 1350 BC, which weighs over 11 kilograms and is made of solid gold with inlays of lapis lazuli, carnelian, and turquoise. We also have a collection of twenty-three canopic jars, which were used to store the internal organs of the deceased during the mummification process, and a beautifully preserved Book of the Dead papyrus scroll measuring over twelve metres in length. Gallery Five is dedicated entirely to the discovery and legacy of Tutankhamun's tomb. Although the actual treasures from Tutankhamun's tomb remain in Egypt, this gallery features high-quality replicas alongside historical photographs and documents from Howard Carter's 1922 excavation. You can see a full-scale reproduction of the inner burial chamber and learn about the painstaking process of cataloguing and conserving the more than 5,000 objects found within the tomb. Galleries Six and Seven explore daily life in ancient Egypt, including sections on agriculture, medicine, writing, and religion. One of the most fascinating objects in this section is a complete set of surgical instruments dating from approximately 1500 BC, demonstrating the remarkable sophistication of ancient Egyptian medicine. We also have an extensive collection of shabti figurines, which were placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife. The final gallery, Gallery Eight, examines Egypt's influence on the modern world, from the Egyptomania that swept Europe in the early nineteenth century following Napoleon's Egyptian campaign to contemporary popular culture. This gallery includes early copies of the Rosetta Stone, Victorian-era archaeological equipment, and film posters from classic Egyptian-themed movies. The exhibition will run from this Saturday, the 12th of October, through to the 28th of February next year. Opening hours are Tuesday to Sunday, 10 AM to 5 PM, with late opening until 8 PM on Thursdays. The museum is closed on Mondays. Admission is twelve pounds for adults, eight pounds for students and seniors, and free for children under twelve. Audio guides are available in eight languages, including Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, and Arabic, for an additional four pounds. Guided tours led by our expert curators are available daily at 11 AM and 2 PM, and are included in the admission price.

sections.passage: A discussion between two students, Hana and David, and their supervisor, Professor Williams, about their biology research project on marine ecosystems and coral reef degradation. Hana begins by presenting their research question: what are the primary factors contributing to coral bleaching events, and how effective are current conservation strategies in mitigating these effects? She explains that they have conducted a comprehensive literature review and gathered preliminary data from three research sites in the Indo-Pacific region. Professor Williams asks about their key findings from the literature review. David responds that the primary driver of coral bleaching is elevated sea surface temperature caused by climate change. He explains that corals have a symbiotic relationship with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which live within coral tissue and provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. When water temperatures rise by just one to two degrees Celsius above the normal summer maximum for a period of several weeks, corals become stressed and expel the zooxanthellae, causing them to turn white, an event known as bleaching. Without the algae, the coral begins to starve and, if conditions do not improve within a few weeks, the coral dies. Hana adds that between 2014 and 2017, the world experienced the longest and most widespread coral bleaching event ever recorded, affecting approximately 75 percent of the world's tropical reefs. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the world's largest coral reef system, was particularly hard hit, with approximately 50 percent of its shallow-water corals dying during this period. Professor Williams acknowledges the severity of the problem and asks about other contributing factors. David explains that in addition to rising temperatures, coral reefs face multiple stressors including ocean acidification, which reduces the ability of corals to build their calcium carbonate skeletons, as well as pollution from agricultural runoff, overfishing that disrupts ecosystem balance, and physical damage from coastal development and tourism. He mentions that ocean pH has decreased by approximately 0.1 units since the pre-industrial era, representing a 26 percent increase in acidity, and is projected to decrease by a further 0.3 to 0.4 units by 2100 under current emission scenarios. The discussion then turns to conservation strategies. Hana describes three main approaches that have been implemented worldwide. The first is the establishment of Marine Protected Areas, or MPAs, where human activities are restricted to allow ecosystems to recover. She cites a 2022 meta-analysis of 150 MPAs globally that found coral cover within protected areas was on average 25 percent higher than in comparable unprotected areas. The second approach involves coral restoration programmes, where fragments of healthy coral are cultivated in underwater nurseries and then transplanted onto degraded reefs. She mentions a successful project in the Caribbean that has transplanted over 100,000 coral fragments across degraded reef sites, with a survival rate of approximately 75 percent after two years. The third approach focuses on reducing local stressors such as pollution and overfishing, thereby increasing the resilience of coral reefs to withstand climate-related bleaching events. Professor Williams raises the emerging field of assisted evolution, which involves selectively breeding corals for heat tolerance or exposing them to gradually increasing temperatures to enhance their thermal resilience. She mentions research being conducted at the Australian Institute of Marine Science, where scientists have successfully produced coral offspring that can tolerate temperatures one to two degrees higher than their parents. However, she cautions that this approach is still experimental and raises ethical questions about the genetic modification of wild ecosystems. The group agrees that their report should present a balanced assessment of these different strategies and conclude with evidence-based recommendations. They set a timeline with a preliminary report due in four weeks and the final paper due eight weeks from today. Professor Williams also suggests they attend a guest lecture next Thursday by Dr. Maria Santos, a leading coral reef ecologist from the University of Queensland, who will be speaking about her latest research findings.

sections.passage: A university lecture on the psychology and anthropology of human migration and cultural adaptation. Good afternoon. Today's lecture explores the psychological and cultural dimensions of human migration, examining how individuals and communities adapt when they move from one cultural environment to another. This is a topic of increasing relevance in a world where an estimated 281 million people, approximately 3.6 percent of the global population, live outside their country of birth. Let us begin with the concept of culture shock, a term coined by the anthropologist Kalervo Oberg in 1960. Oberg described culture shock as a four-stage process that most people experience when they immerse themselves in an unfamiliar culture. The first stage, the honeymoon phase, is characterised by excitement and fascination with the new culture. Everything seems fresh and interesting, and differences between the home culture and the new culture are perceived positively. This phase typically lasts from a few weeks to several months. The second stage, the crisis or frustration phase, is when the differences between cultures begin to cause genuine difficulty. Language barriers, unfamiliar social customs, and feelings of isolation can lead to anxiety, homesickness, and frustration. This is the most challenging phase and typically occurs between three and six months after arrival. The third stage, adjustment, involves gradually developing coping strategies and a more balanced understanding of the new culture. Individuals begin to navigate cultural differences more effectively and may develop routines and social networks that provide stability. The final stage, adaptation, represents a state of relative comfort and competence in the new culture, though Oberg noted that most migrants never achieve complete cultural integration and instead develop a bicultural or multicultural identity. More recent research has refined and, in some cases, challenged Oberg's original model. The sociocultural adaptation model developed by Colleen Ward and colleagues proposes that successful adaptation involves two distinct but related dimensions: psychological adaptation, which relates to emotional wellbeing and life satisfaction, and sociocultural adaptation, which involves the ability to navigate daily life in the new culture, including understanding social norms, communicating effectively, and forming relationships. Ward's research found that while psychological adaptation tends to follow the U-shaped curve described by Oberg, sociocultural adaptation typically improves more steadily over time, with the most rapid gains occurring in the first year. Language acquisition is perhaps the most critical factor in cultural adaptation. Research consistently shows that proficiency in the host country's language is the strongest predictor of both psychological and sociocultural adaptation. A 2019 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, which examined 85 studies involving over 40,000 participants, found that language proficiency had a correlation coefficient of 0.48 with overall adaptation, significantly higher than any other variable studied, including length of residence, age, education level, and social support networks. The role of social identity in the migration experience is another important area of research. John Berry's acculturation framework identifies four strategies that migrants may adopt when navigating between their heritage culture and the host culture: integration, where individuals maintain their heritage culture while also adopting aspects of the host culture; assimilation, where individuals abandon their heritage culture and fully adopt the host culture; separation, where individuals maintain their heritage culture and avoid interaction with the host culture; and marginalisation, where individuals lose connection with both cultures. Berry's research across numerous countries has consistently found that integration is associated with the best psychological and sociocultural outcomes, while marginalisation is associated with the worst. The experiences of second-generation immigrants, those born in the host country to immigrant parents, present unique psychological challenges. These individuals often navigate what researchers call the acculturation gap, a discrepancy between their own cultural adaptation and that of their parents. While second-generation children typically adapt quickly to the host culture through schooling and peer interactions, their parents may retain stronger ties to the heritage culture. This gap can lead to intergenerational conflict and identity confusion, as young people feel caught between two sets of cultural expectations. A 2021 study across twelve European countries found that 62 percent of second-generation immigrants reported experiencing significant identity conflicts related to their dual cultural heritage. The economic dimension of migration also has profound psychological effects. Research shows that the psychological impact of migration depends heavily on whether the move was voluntary or forced. Voluntary migrants, who choose to move for economic opportunity or personal reasons, generally experience better psychological outcomes than refugees and asylum seekers, who have been forced to flee their homes due to conflict, persecution, or natural disaster. A 2022 meta-analysis by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees found that rates of post-traumatic stress disorder among refugee populations were approximately five times higher than among voluntary migrants, and rates of depression were approximately three times higher. Community-level factors also play crucial roles in migrant adaptation. Migrants who settle in areas with established diaspora communities from their home country tend to adapt more quickly, as these communities provide cultural familiarity, practical support, and emotional comfort during the transition period. However, over-reliance on diaspora communities can also slow cultural adaptation to the host society if it reduces incentives to learn the host language and engage with the broader community. The concept of transnationalism, the maintenance of active social, economic, and cultural connections with the home country while living abroad, has become increasingly prevalent in the age of digital communication. Migrants can now participate in family events via video call, consume media from their home country, and maintain political engagement in their country of origin through online platforms. This has led some researchers to argue that the traditional model of linear assimilation is being replaced by a more fluid, circular model of cultural engagement, where migrants move between cultural identities rather than transitioning from one to another.

title.en: Passage 1 - The History and Science of Vaccination
title.zh: 文章1 - 疫苗接种的历史与科学

sections.passage: Vaccination is widely regarded as one of the most important public health interventions in human history, having saved an estimated 154 million lives over the past fifty years, according to the World Health Organisation. The principle behind vaccination is elegantly simple: by exposing the immune system to a weakened, inactivated, or partial form of a pathogen, the body learns to recognise and fight the disease without experiencing its full effects. This process of building immunity has enabled the eradication of smallpox, the near-elimination of polio, and the dramatic reduction of numerous other infectious diseases. The practice of inducing immunity has ancient roots. As early as the tenth century, Chinese physicians practised a technique called variolation, in which material from smallpox scabs was blown into the nostrils of healthy individuals to produce a mild form of the disease and subsequent immunity. Similar practices were documented in India, the Ottoman Empire, and Africa. However, the modern era of vaccination began in 1796, when the English physician Edward Jenner conducted his famous experiment. Jenner observed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease, appeared to be immune to smallpox, a devastating illness that killed approximately 30 percent of those infected. He tested his hypothesis by inoculating an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps, with material from a cowpox lesion and later exposing him to smallpox. The boy did not develop the disease, demonstrating that cowpox provided protection against smallpox. Jenner's work laid the foundation for the development of vaccines against many other diseases. The nineteenth century saw rapid advances in vaccine development, driven by the work of pioneering scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch. Pasteur developed vaccines against rabies and anthrax, while his contemporary Koch identified the bacteria responsible for tuberculosis and cholera, enabling more targeted approaches to immunisation. The invention of laboratory techniques for growing and attenuating, or weakening, pathogens was a crucial breakthrough, allowing scientists to produce vaccines that were safe enough for widespread use. The twentieth century witnessed an explosion of vaccine development that transformed global health. Vaccines were developed against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, measles, mumps, rubella, and hepatitis B, among others. The global smallpox eradication campaign, led by the WHO from 1967 to 1980, remains the greatest achievement of vaccination, resulting in the complete elimination of a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. The development of the polio vaccines by Jonas Salk in 1955 and Albert Sabin in 1961 brought a crippling disease under control in much of the world, and polio is now endemic in only two countries: Afghanistan and Pakistan. The mechanism of vaccination involves several key components of the immune system. When a vaccine is administered, the antigens it contains are recognised by specialised white blood cells called antigen-presenting cells, which process the antigens and present them to T cells and B cells. T cells coordinate the immune response and can directly kill infected cells, while B cells produce antibodies, proteins that specifically recognise and neutralise the pathogen. Crucially, after the initial immune response, a subset of T cells and B cells become memory cells that persist in the body for years or even decades, enabling a rapid and robust response if the individual encounters the actual pathogen in the future. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated vaccine technology in unprecedented ways. The development of mRNA vaccines by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna represented a revolutionary approach to immunisation. Unlike traditional vaccines, which use weakened or inactivated pathogens, mRNA vaccines deliver genetic instructions that teach cells to produce a harmless piece of the virus, triggering an immune response. This technology, which had been in development for over two decades, proved remarkably effective and was deployed in record time: the first COVID-19 vaccine received emergency use authorisation less than a year after the virus was identified. The success of mRNA technology has opened new possibilities for vaccine development against other diseases, including malaria, HIV, and various types of cancer. Despite the overwhelming evidence of vaccination's benefits, vaccine hesitancy has emerged as a significant public health concern. The WHO listed vaccine hesitancy as one of the top ten threats to global health in 2019, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. Factors contributing to vaccine hesitancy include misinformation spread through social media, historical instances of medical malpractice that have eroded trust in health institutions, and genuine concerns about rare side effects. Addressing vaccine hesitancy requires transparent communication about both the benefits and risks of vaccination, culturally sensitive outreach, and sustained investment in public health infrastructure.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Impact of Space Exploration on Everyday Life
title.zh: 文章2 - 太空探索对日常生活的影响

sections.passage: When most people think of space exploration, they imagine astronauts floating in zero gravity, rovers traversing the surface of Mars, or spectacular rocket launches. What is less commonly appreciated is the profound and pervasive impact that space technology has on everyday life on Earth. From the memory foam in your mattress to the GPS navigation in your car, many technologies that we take for granted originated from or were significantly advanced by space research. The relationship between space exploration and terrestrial technology dates back to the earliest days of the space race. When NASA was established in 1958, one of its founding mandates was to share the technological benefits of space research with the wider public. This commitment led to the creation of the Technology Transfer Programme, which has facilitated the commercialisation of thousands of space-derived technologies. NASA's annual publication, Spinoff, has documented over 2,000 such technologies since its first edition in 1976. Perhaps the most ubiquitous space-derived technology is the Global Positioning System, or GPS. Originally developed by the United States Department of Defense for military navigation, GPS relies on a constellation of 24 satellites orbiting the Earth at an altitude of approximately 20,200 kilometres. Each satellite broadcasts precise timing signals, and a GPS receiver on the ground calculates its position by comparing the time signals from multiple satellites. While GPS was initially restricted to military use, it was made available for civilian applications in 1983 following the shooting down of a Korean Air Lines flight that had strayed into Soviet airspace due to a navigation error. Today, GPS technology supports an estimated four billion users worldwide and underpins critical infrastructure including aviation, maritime navigation, agriculture, emergency services, and telecommunications. The estimated economic value of GPS to the US economy alone is approximately 1.4 trillion dollars since its civilian introduction. Water purification technology is another area where space research has made significant terrestrial contributions. In the 1960s, NASA developed advanced water filtration systems for the Apollo missions to ensure astronauts had access to clean drinking water in space. These systems, which used iodine and activated carbon to remove contaminants, were subsequently adapted for use in developing countries where access to clean water is limited. Today, spin-off water purification technology based on NASA's designs provides clean drinking water to millions of people in over 80 countries. One notable example is the Microbial Check Valve, a device originally designed for the Space Shuttle that has been adapted into portable water purification units used in disaster relief operations and rural communities worldwide. Medical technology has also benefited enormously from space research. The digital image processing techniques originally developed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory to enhance images of the Moon's surface were later adapted for use in medical imaging, including CT scans and MRI technology. Infrared thermometers, now ubiquitous in hospitals and homes, derive from technology developed to measure the temperature of stars and planets. Robotic surgery systems, which allow surgeons to perform complex procedures with enhanced precision, have roots in the robotic arm technology developed for the Space Shuttle and International Space Station. Even the humble cochlear implant, which has restored hearing to hundreds of thousands of people worldwide, benefited from NASA's research into miniaturised electronics for space applications. Materials science represents perhaps the most widespread category of space spin-offs. Memory foam, originally developed by NASA in the 1966 to improve crash protection for airline pilots, is now used in mattresses, pillows, shoes, and medical equipment worldwide. Scratch-resistant coatings for eyeglasses were derived from astronaut helmet visor technology. Space suits, which must protect astronauts from extreme temperatures ranging from minus 157 to 121 degrees Celsius, have inspired advanced insulation materials now used in winter clothing and firefighting equipment. The heat-resistant materials developed for spacecraft re-entry have found applications in industrial furnaces, racing car components, and protective equipment for firefighters. The International Space Station, which has been continuously occupied since November 2000, serves as a unique laboratory for scientific research that cannot be conducted on Earth. Experiments in microgravity have led to advances in drug development, materials science, and our understanding of fundamental biological processes. For example, protein crystal growth experiments conducted on the ISS have produced larger and more perfect protein crystals than can be grown on Earth, enabling scientists to better understand the structure of proteins associated with diseases such as muscular dystrophy and Duchenne disease. This research has directly contributed to the development of new pharmaceutical treatments. Looking to the future, the emerging commercial space industry promises to generate even more technological spin-offs. Companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Virgin Galactic are dramatically reducing the cost of space access, while space tourism, asteroid mining, and the establishment of permanent lunar and Martian bases could drive innovation in life support systems, renewable energy, construction materials, and agricultural technologies that would benefit life on Earth.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Global Coffee Industry: Past, Present, and Future
title.zh: 文章3 - 全球咖啡产业：过去、现在和未来

sections.passage: Coffee is one of the most widely traded commodities on Earth, with an estimated 2.25 billion cups consumed every day across the globe. The global coffee industry is valued at approximately 495 billion dollars annually and supports the livelihoods of an estimated 125 million people, predominantly smallholder farmers in developing countries. Yet despite its ubiquity in modern life, the coffee industry faces unprecedented challenges that threaten its long-term sustainability. The origins of coffee drinking are steeped in legend and debate. The most popular story, likely apocryphal, involves an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi who noticed his goats became unusually energetic after eating berries from a particular tree. Whether or not this story is true, Ethiopia is widely recognised as the birthplace of coffee, and the plant Coffea arabica originated in the highlands of eastern Africa. By the fifteenth century, coffee drinking had spread to the Arabian Peninsula, where coffee houses, known as qahveh khaneh, became important centres of social activity, intellectual discourse, and political debate. The seventeenth century saw coffee arrive in Europe, where it quickly became fashionable. Coffee houses sprang up in major cities across the continent, becoming hubs of commerce, creativity, and conversation. Lloyd's of London, the famous insurance market, began as a coffee house in 1688. The Parisian café culture that persists to this day has its roots in the coffee houses of the same era. European colonial powers, recognising the commercial potential of coffee, began cultivating it in their tropical colonies, establishing plantation systems in Java, Ceylon, Brazil, and the Caribbean. These colonial plantations relied heavily on slave labour and later on indentured workers, a dark chapter in coffee's history that continues to shape the industry's power dynamics. Today, Brazil is by far the world's largest coffee producer, accounting for approximately 37 percent of global production, followed by Vietnam at 16 percent, Colombia at 7 percent, and Indonesia at 6 percent. However, the vast majority of coffee farmers are smallholders cultivating plots of fewer than five hectares. These farmers typically earn only 10 percent of the retail price of their coffee, with the remaining value captured by processors, traders, roasters, and retailers in consuming countries. This disparity has fuelled the fair trade movement, which guarantees farmers a minimum price for their coffee and promotes more equitable trading relationships. The fair trade coffee market has grown significantly since its inception in the late 1980s, with certified sales reaching approximately 1.3 billion dollars in 2022. Climate change poses the most significant existential threat to the coffee industry. The two main species cultivated commercially, Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora, commonly known as robusta, are both highly sensitive to changes in temperature, rainfall, and humidity. Arabica, which accounts for approximately 60 percent of global production and is prized for its complex flavour profile, grows best at temperatures between 18 and 22 degrees Celsius and is particularly vulnerable to rising temperatures. A 2022 study published in the journal PLOS ONE projected that by 2050, the amount of land suitable for growing arabica coffee could decrease by approximately 50 percent under moderate climate change scenarios and by up to 80 percent under severe scenarios. Robusta, while more resilient to heat, is sensitive to drought and is also expected to face significant production challenges. The impact of climate change on coffee production is already being observed. In Brazil, severe frosts in 2021 destroyed approximately 11 percent of the country's coffee plants, causing global coffee prices to spike by over 40 percent. In Central America, the spread of coffee leaf rust, a fungal disease exacerbated by changing climate conditions, has devastated plantations across the region, forcing thousands of farmers to abandon coffee cultivation. The World Coffee Research organisation estimates that by 2050, up to 50 percent of the land currently used for coffee production may become unsuitable without significant adaptation measures. In response to these challenges, researchers and industry stakeholders are pursuing several strategies. Climate-resilient coffee varieties are being developed through both traditional breeding techniques and genetic research. World Coffee Research has developed over 60 experimental hybrid varieties that combine the flavour quality of arabica with the climate resilience of robusta. Agroforestry, the practice of growing coffee under a canopy of shade trees, is being promoted as a way to moderate temperatures, reduce water stress, and sequester carbon. Studies have shown that shade-grown coffee can be two to four degrees cooler than coffee grown in full sun, providing a buffer against rising temperatures. The specialty coffee movement, which emphasises quality, origin, and unique flavour profiles, has also emerged as a potential saviour for the industry. By commanding premium prices, specialty coffee can provide farmers with higher incomes that enable investment in sustainable practices. The global specialty coffee market was valued at approximately 83 billion dollars in 2023 and is growing at a rate of approximately 12 percent per year. Direct trade relationships between roasters and farmers, bypassing traditional intermediaries, are becoming increasingly common and can return up to 50 percent of the retail price to the farmer, compared to the typical 10 percent.

prompt.en:
The maps below show a coastal town called Pebbleton in 2000 and the proposed changes for 2025.

2000: A small fishing harbour with a fish market on the waterfront. A main road runs through the town centre with local shops and a town hall. Residential houses are located to the north. A primary school is in the northeast corner. Farmland occupies the eastern section.

2025 Proposed Changes: The fishing harbour will be replaced by a modern marina with restaurants and a hotel. The fish market will become a shopping centre. The main road will be widened and a new bypass road will be built around the town. The farmland in the east will be converted into a housing estate with 200 new homes. A new secondary school will be built adjacent to the primary school. A leisure centre with a swimming pool will be constructed near the marina.

Summarise the changes by selecting and reporting the main features. Write at least 150 words.
